extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy/epistemology (early modern philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying John Locke's taxonomy and evaluative distinctions among ideas (real vs fantastical, adequate vs inadequate, true vs false, simple vs complex, modes vs substances) as presented in this chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas which have a foundation in nature; such as have a conformity with the real being and existence of things, or with their archetypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Real ideas correspond to powers or constitutions of things outside the mind; simple ideas as effects of powers in things are examples of real ideas. They function as reliable distinguishing characters insofar as they are steadily produced by external causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fantastical (chimerical) ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas which have no foundation in nature, nor any conformity with the reality of being to which they are tacitly referred (their supposed archetypes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are combinations not matching any real pattern or are inconsistent/jumbled ideas (e.g., a rational creature with a horse's head joined to a human body). Such ideas should be treated as imaginary and not reliable representations of real substances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple ideas are real and adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: All our simple ideas are real appearances of things and are adequate, because they are effects of powers in things fitted to produce such sensations in us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple ideas (e.g., whiteness, heat) cannot be produced by the mind itself and therefore correspond to real powers in external objects; as such they perfectly represent those powers insofar as the sensation is the intended object of the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas are voluntary combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas are combinations of simple ideas put together by the mind; the mind uses some liberty in forming them, so individuals' complex ideas (e.g., of gold or justice) can differ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex ideas may be real or fantastical depending on whether the combination corresponds to something possible or existing. The mind's freedom in assembling simple ideas is the source of variation and potential error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed modes and relations (real when possible)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes and relations, being collections of consistent ideas, are real so long as there is a possibility of existing conformable to them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These ideas are archetypes created by the mind; they count as real if they could correspond to a possible mode (e.g., a composed idea of a particular kind of action). Their fantasticalness is often a matter of improper naming rather than metaphysical impossibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex ideas of substances are real when they agree with existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of substances are intended to represent substances as they really are and are real only insofar as they are combinations of simple ideas that actually co-exist in things without us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the combination mirrors what exists externally it is real; if it consists of qualities never found together, it is fantastical. However, the chapter goes on to argue substantial limits on adequacy here (see related metrics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequate ideas defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequate ideas are such as perfectly represent the archetypes (what the mind supposes them to be taken from).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adequate idea contains all that the mind intends it to represent. Simple ideas and true archetypal modes meet this standard; complex ideas of substances typically do not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inadequate ideas defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Inadequate ideas are partial or incomplete representations of the archetypes to which they are referred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many complex ideas (especially of substances) are inadequate because they omit aspects of the real essence or powers of things; inadequacy often arises when an idea is meant to correspond to unknown essences or to another person's mental pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes (complex ideas of modes) are adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of modes, being created by the mind as archetypes without reference to external patterns, cannot but be adequate to the mind's intention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because modes are designed to be patterns the mind itself intends, these complex ideas contain precisely what was intended and so are complete in that sense (e.g., the idea of a triangle as three sides and three angles).

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes may be inadequate relative to settled names
rubrics_metrics.description: Modes (mixed modes) can become inadequate if, in social use, a person’s idea diverges from the settled idea associated with a common name (i.e., failure to correspond to other men's ideas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inadequacy here is a matter of linguistic/proprietary correctness: if one uses the same name but has a different internal complex idea, their idea fails to match the communal archetype and is therefore inadequate for communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances are not adequate to real essences
rubrics_metrics.description: Our complex ideas of substances are inadequate when referred to supposed real essences because we do not know those essences and hence cannot represent them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People commonly assume names refer to real internal essences; since those essences are unknown, ideas meant to correspond to them necessarily fall short. Invoking 'substantial forms' does not remedy this ignorance because no clear idea of such essences is available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of substances (as collections of qualities) are inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when complex ideas of substances are formed by collecting sensible qualities, they remain inadequate because no one includes all the simple ideas (powers/properties) that belong to that substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because substances have numerous powers discoverable only by varied interactions, any finite collection of observed qualities in a person's idea will omit others; therefore such complex ideas cannot fully represent the substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substances have innumerable powers beyond our ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual substances possess many properties not contained in a typical complex idea (e.g., far more properties of gold exist than the few commonly abstracted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This point supports the inadequacy thesis: detailed empirical investigation reveals many properties omitted from ordinary ideas, so complex ideas of substances underrepresent their archetypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes and relations are archetypes; substances are ectypes
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex ideas of modes and relations are originals (archetypes) made by the mind and so are adequate; complex ideas of substances are copies (ectypes) intended to copy external substances and so are liable to inadequacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction explains why modes can be complete and self-sufficient whereas ideas of substances, as copies of external essences, are necessarily incomplete relative to what they aim to represent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth and falsehood belong properly to propositions, not ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and falsehood properly attach to PROPOSITIONS; ideas as bare mental appearances are not, in themselves, true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call an idea 'true' only in a metaphysical sense of existence, but in ordinary epistemic use truth/falsity arises when the mind makes an affirmation or negation (a tacit proposition) about the idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas become true/false when referred beyond themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: An idea may be called true or false when the mind refers it to something extraneous (other men's ideas, real existence, or supposed real essences); the tacit supposition of conformity is what can be true or false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Three common cases: (1) referring an idea to the idea in other men's minds (linguistic agreement), (2) referring an idea to real existence (does it correspond to something real?), (3) referring an idea to a supposed real essence (does it match the unknown essence?). Only under such references can an idea be judged true or false.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideas of infinite or actual infinite (eternity, infinite divisibility) are obscure and lead to confusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Because our ideas are finite, when we talk of eternity or infinite divisibility we cannot form a clear, distinct positive idea of the whole infinite; parts beyond our conceivable bounds remain obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argumentation about infinities tends to produce blunders and manifest absurdities because our mental ideas lack determinate content for the actually infinite; we only have relative, comparative, or numeric notions, not clear positive ideas of actual infinity.
